> TL;DR: GNU Savannah hosts Bash, Coreutils, and hundreds of other GNU projects. Using Hacktron, we found that an email address like a`touch${IFS}/tmp/savane-rce-proof`@attacker.example gave any registered user code execution on its backend. An unpatched kernel gave us root access and access to a GNU backup server. We reported it to the FSF on May 11, 2026.

> Like much of the infrastructure free software depends on, it’s run by a handful of volunteers and FSF staff with limited resources. We wanted to put our resources to work there. Savannah runs Savane, a PHP application that is itself free software, so we pointed Hacktron at the source and audited it.

Imagine attackers reading that and ordering swarms of abliterated frontier models onto an open source project like that.

Many projects like the FSF do not use AI themselves maybe "by principle", but the attackers don't care and will unleash AI agents on to anyone as a backdoor target.

Given all that you have seen with the mass discovery of these security issues and hacks, there will be no choice from open source projects to conglomerates to use AI to protect themselves ahead of the attackers.

I can say specific to AI: I have been seeing friends and colleagues do really impressive things with code surpassing what's available in the market and open source in the past few months. The vast majority of them are _not_ releasing their code, for a variety of reasons:

- Their output is hyper-customized/optimized for their personal use case, constraints and quirks

- They have zero interest in being an open source contributor and maintainer. Usually because it's a lot of additional work, sometimes for personal safety reasons (harassment targets etc.) In a workplace it can also mean dealing with an extremely tedious legal process with months of uncertainty.

- They figure anyone who wants something similar can just make it themselves instead of using theirs. If I spent between fifteen minutes and two days to make some software, in 3-6 months someone with fewer skills will probably make it in 5 minutes to a few hours using a more powerful model.

- They may not have full rights to redistribute their source code.

Basically most people - individuals and corporations alike - aren't actually interested in donating to open source and in many cases have anti-incentives to do so.

comment_text.value:
> Someone who is using a residential proxy network, headless browsing, and/or TLS fingerprint manipulation to evade rate limits and other controls to issue large volumes of automated requests under a deceptive UserAgent string isn't difficult to describe and differentiate versus a normal user using a UA.

So then why isn't it trying to prohibit making multiple requests from different IP addresses in a residential proxy network, rather than the thing it actually does?

> The proposed text of the bill is rather straightforward. It turns more on the "stealth" bit than "bot".

Not really, look at the definition of "STEALTH BOT" -- the only thing that nominally distinguishes it from a browser is the word "bot" which isn't itself defined, because the phrase "without prior disclosure of its identity and purpose" is something that a normal web browser doesn't do either.

It can't even get it out of it via "a valid and accurate user-agent string", both because that clause says or and it still fails the second one, and because "a valid and accurate user-agent string" is a nonsense phrase. The Safari user agent strings start with "Mozilla" even though it's not. The Android ones do the same and then include "AppleWebKit" and "Mobile Safari" too. A browser extension uses the user agent string of the browser regardless of what the extension does. When Debian packages their version of Firefox, its user agent string says Firefox and not Debian.

User agent strings don't have a registry. "Valid" has no meaning and "accurate" is contrary to the default behavior of common browsers.

comment_text.value:
Anyone can make their own emulator. The ISA is publicly documented, and MCU datasheets are also public. There are also open source emulators like Renode and QEMU, like we wrote in our post. I would say there are two main differences between us and you using Claude to make its own emulator:

1. Although the ISA and peripheral behavior for the MCUs are documented, there are hardware intricacies that can't be effectively done with just an LLM. Things like register transaction timings, and hardware bugs (yes chip designers make mistakes in designs that aren't shown in documentation) requires many weeks of constant bench testing to detect and fix.

2. Maintenance. Yes, Claude is incredibly good. But it still makes mistakes. We understand that, and we're always making updates to our simulation software whenever there is a bug. You however, as a firmware engineer whose job is to make products and ship code, I would assume you would rather work on that instead spending all day fixing and updating a simulator. We do the maintenance for you, so you can focus on building your things.

Hope that answers your question! We're not claiming that AI can't do it with enough time and resources. It's just that the people who find value in this would rather spend their time on other things.

comment_text.value:
> So first of all what crisis are we talking about here, a fiscal crisis

France is in the red and bailing it out would put require all members to pool money (unlikely) or print money (causing inflation).

If you think that printing money is free win consider that non-EU countries aren't stupid, they will demand more EUR for their goods. Which might require another round of money printing.

> And can you spell out the exact connection to

Yeah, it's called Euro Zone. Look this wasn't some deep thought. Whatever one country in EZ does impacts others through the shared currency. If say Italy and France need to be bailed out this causes EUR to depreciate (hurting importers), and if say Germany and Poland are doing extremely good it causes EUR to appreciate (hurting exporters).

> We don't have a Gambia here

Sure we do. Gambia is a real country and it could peg their currency. This happens often during crises of currency trust.

However, pegging Gambia's currency to USD only works in short terms. If their policies aren't aligned and there is no money redistributions, Gambia will sooner or later have to float their currency.

This is nutshell what France was doing (on a less apparent scale). It was pegging its weaker currency to EUR (because it's a large importer). An importer loves strong currency, but importing too much devalues your currency, which would prevent overspending because the more you import the less profitable it is to import. A similar thing happens to exporters but their currency appreciates.

> Can you without looking it up say which EU member produces the most cars per capita?

No idea, my original guess would be Poland or some poorer country. Having checked it's Germany. I don't quite see the convergence this is supposed to show.

> to freely (as freely as possible) doing business across internal EU borders, in this case

That's a nice to have, but not necessary. I count prosperity and life satisfaction more important than free trade.

comment_text.value: Centralized stablecoins like USDT and USDC aren't layer-one cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. They're more like applications running on top of other blockchains, usually as smart contracts, and their issuers hold admin keys which can freeze, mint, burn, and otherwise redistribute funds at will. As far as timing goes, stablecoin issuers can't actually cancel or reverse a transaction that's already in a block that's been mined, but they can freeze the receiving address afterward and burn the funds there, then reissue them elsewhere, which has much the same effect.

comment_text.value:
Have you noted that in the mainline Linux build config file, the option to enable IPv4 functionality is CONFIG_LEGACY_IP= ?

I can tell you that in cicd for production Linux systems today, we have

  CONFIG_LEGACY_IP=""
which in a Linux build config file means "do not include this in the build".

_

What might work well for your organization is ZeroTier which will make you immune to what any ISPs do. The downside is your organization would be dependent on ZeroTier, but ZeroTier is much less likely to screw you over than any ISP.

  https://www.zerotier.com/
_

I appreciate your speculation on the principles of contract law. Like you, I believe those principles should be upheld and I believe in morality. If you lived under a monarchy and I were of the monarch, I would cross-examine your ISP in public and solve your problem in minutes. I would also on occasion take someone to the side of the road and chop off their head in front of the entire village, and everyone would know on a visceral level they are all much better off with someone taking out the trash now and then.

But, as many technical workers know, the contract stuff takes months or years to resolve, and technical issues involving IP addresses are best worked around with technical approaches.

_

What I would suggest your network team (you and whoever) do in your shoes is:

- set up NAT64 and DNS64 at the edges of subnets that contain devices that don't do IPv6 properly, because if these devices do not have updates to do IPv6 properly then they are broken in a fundamental way, and a workaround is necessary;

- dictate that starting on December 1st, all new devices and VMs have IPv6 addresses with all userspace services listening on IPv6 addresses or some nftables rule to kludge IPv6:$port -> 127.0.0.1:$port if necessary, with firewall configured to block that IPv6 traffic, then at a later date firewalls not blocking those IPv6 addresses, then at a later date prohibit any new IPv4 addresses being assigned anywhere with special exception to devices tagged "legacy" or "end of life" requiring documentation of such;

- use a combination of IPv6 GUA addresses assigned by whatever ISP and IPv6 ULA addresses chosen by your team -- in IPv6, multiple local gateways and multiple addresses on a network interface issued by those local gateways via RA is relatively a norm rather than an exception (requires userspace tooling in IPv4, DHCP doesn't have this functionality), so leverage this advantage;

- use IPv6 AH (authenticated headers) wherever possible;

- because in an ideal world, ISPs would behave consistently and IPv6 GUA addresses would always be stable, but we aren't living in an ideal world, so be ready to update your internal DNS to drop AAAA records containing IPv6 GUA that an upstream ISP fumbled;

- or, if you have the internal resources, register your own AS and command your own official block of IPv6 addresses;

- use a combination of OpenTOFU (Terraform) and Salt or Ansible, all versioned with Git, be very strict with your team about versioning with Git, to manage everything, and use

  terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
and Salt or Ansible equivalents for continuous monitoring;

- move userspace services to Podman where possible.

Personally I like Salt. I know Ansible is more popular out there with more inertia.

_

>> why are we normalizing the removal of IPv4 addresses?

This was normalized a long time ago actually. "The future is already here, it's just not evenly distributed".

You and I are total strangers on different corners of the globe. You may not like what you're about to read, but it's better that you get a hint where the wind is blowing sooner than not.

If my team were consulting with your organization's execs and we caught a hint that the existing internal resources were not already proactively staying current with internet protocol (which is IPv6), we would point out there is urgency to start right away with emphasis that the existing internal team is over two decades behind staying current.

Or, if a detected hint the internal team were at all resistant to IPv6, we would advise the executive team to start developing a plan to flush out the replacements for the internal team ASAP.

Many network engineers at many ISPs would gladly drop all IPv4 traffic if they thought they could get away with it.

IPv6 only seems more complicated if you still need to unlearn IPv4. IPv6 does have a steeper learning curve, but once that learning curve is overcome, IPv6 is actually much simpler than IPv4. More people than not don't like reading RFCs, but professionals do slowly read RFCs on their own time.

and Salt or Ansible equivalents for continuous monitoring;

You and I are total strangers on different corners of the globe. You may not like what you're about to read, but it's better that you get a hint where the wind is blowing sooner than not.

If my team were consulting with your organization's execs and we caught a hint that the existing internal resources were not already proactively staying current with internet protocol (which is IPv6), we would point out there is urgency to start right away with emphasis that the existing internal team is over two decades behind staying current.

If you leave the door to your house unlocked, am I welcome to come in, pop on into your utility closet, plug into a switch port and take everything your machines allow me to fetch?

I don't disagree with what he was doing from a moral standpoint or a hacker standpoint, but it's very easy to convict him.

This discussion typically devolves into an argument about what is "publicly accessible." No reasonable person (i.e. those who serve on juries - not autistic software engineers) would agree that someone who isn't even a student at a school is legally entitled to enter a building (unlocked or not), venture into their utility room and access protected computer resources.

Everyone loves to make this about JSTOR: they weren't the only victim. MIT was far more aggrieved; JSTOR blocking his Harvard account access and him proceeding to breach their TOS ("clickwrap agreements aren't law!!!") and circumvent their defenses isn't required to convict him of CFAA violations.

Why can't I go into a bank, sit down at a personal banker's desk who is away on vacation, plug into a switch port and do whatever I want? There's no lock on his cubicle, the door was open! This is the legal equivalent of "neener neener, I'm not touching you."

Mens rea is an important thing people love to sweep under the rug with this case:

• First and foremost: Why did he have to go to into a closet at MIT to fetch documents? Why not do it at home or a public library?

  • Because of rate limits and/or authentication requirements. He *knew* he could not obtain the access he needed through other means, so he had to trespass to do it.
• Why did he cover his face with his bicycle helmet... just when passing by cameras?

  • He wasn't some weirdo who liked to wear his helmet that way: he stopped immediately when he believed he didn't need to conceal his identity any further. He *knew* he shouldn't be there.
• He registered his guest account using false credentials: "Gary Host" and "Grace Host" - "Ghost"

  • Why wouldn't he just use his real name if he believed what he was doing was legitimate?
• When MIT blocked his IP, he released/renewed and fetched a new one. Fine, no problem on its own, hard to prove intent there. When MIT subsequently blocked his MAC address, he proceeded to change one character and kept on downloading.

  • Computer people will try to reduce this to "MAC addresses aren't legal identifiers blah blah blah." The beliefs of zealous third parties are completely irrelevant: direct measures were taken to prevent his access, he recognized and immediately circumvented them. He *knew* what he was doing. That's what matters.
• Why hide his hardware under boxes? In absence of all of the other facts, sure, one could argue that he didn't want students at this ultra-prestigious Ivy League school to steal his shit, but to a reasonable person weighing the totality of the circumstances: he was again concealing his actions because he knew they were wrong.

I see a lot of police bodycam videos on YouTube of cops stopping drug traffickers for bullshit reasons (5 over speed limit on highway, crossing the line, following too closely) and it's usually a state or county cop that's on a federal task force or they'll have a "civilian ride along" in the car that gets way more involved than any civilian would ever be. They aren't actually an employee of the FBI but they have credentials from the FBI due to their task force job, it gives them access to FBI databases and bulletins while they still maintain their normal police job.

It's really bizarre to watch those videos because they are very routine. Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp, registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread).

Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.)

The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it.

Limits: Threads only. Free plan is 1 account, 3 posts a day and 50 calls a day per live key, and Meta's per-profile caps apply on top. The MCP server lacks the thread, webhook and A/B tools the CLI has. The CLI and bridge are MIT; the service is hosted.

No signup needed to look around: `curl https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp` lists the tools, and `tools/list`, `get_playbook` and `list_formulas` work without a key. A free account gives you a `mt_test_` sandbox key.

A `mt_test_` key simulates every write. Feedback I want: is per-permission ask the right granularity, and what would you need before letting an agent post for you?

comment_text.value:
> What I understand from that is, byte code is portable while machine code isn't.

This is an area I want to explore. It seems to me that it is less true than it used to be. x86_32 was the last significant architecture that made things hard. Now we can ignore that. All desktop or server class CPUs support 8, 16, 32 and 64-bit integers. And they all have at least 10 general purpose registers. They all have a sensible set of memory access modes. As a result, the same code generator works for them all. As it stands, my code generator calls functions like emit_indexed_load, emit_conditional_jump etc. There are currently 26 of those functions and they're all trivial.

So far I have only implemented them for x86_64 machine code output. But writing versions that output ARM64 or risvc doesn't seem hard. I expect I'll find small problems which will cause me to have to tweak the set of CPU features my code gen depends on.

As for generating bytecode being easier than x86_64 machine code, I disagree. There are lots of tools for validating x86_64 machine code (ie disassemblers). There aren't any for a bytecode I might invent. And I can ask an AI how to generate x86_64 machine code to do an indexed load. I immediately get the answer. I don't have to think about how to make an efficient bytecode encoding.

The hardest thing I've encountered so far is getting the ABI right so that my compiled code can call existing functions (eg libc). But I'd have to do that even if I was using an interpreter.

comment_text.value:
A little before that was:

> The most striking feature of agent proofs is that they are verbose, repeatedly spelling out details about the program’s execution: specifying the contents of CPU registers, explicitly writing out integer conversions, explicitly spelling out that many different addresses are all distinct from one another, writing out the exact contents of stack addresses, explicitly considering every possible branch in a function, etc.

> To be sure, these details are important to precisely reason about the execution of code. However, human proof engineers would have immediately introduced abstractions to factor out these types of repetitive specifications.

- - -

This matches my experience when I look at the tests LLMs write to check their own work when I’ve given them a task. The tests are almost universally terrible because they hard code everything in the most brittle way possible. They are nearly useless for regression tests because if I change anything about the source, even in non material ways, the tests all break in stupid ways that aren’t checking any important properties.

If I have the LLM make the then it also has to rewrite all the tests in a new episode of brittle concrete hyper-literal tests. The concept of a regression suite is non-existent.

It’s probably just as well. Having the implementer write the verification is generally a bad idea with people, maybe the problem of carrying over assumptions and blind spots and misconceptions applies to LLMs as well.

One might say it’s operator error, and I’m underspecifying things, but if I have to go to such elaborate lengths to get it to do what I need, I’ll just implement it myself.

> (Moving the PKI into DNS does not remove it, it just moves it around.)

Better in DNS though. You could have certs mirror the structure of DNS. Install a single root signing key for the top level DNS registry on client devices. Then you can query that to find out the signing keys for .com, .net, .au, etc. And continue from there.

One big problem with the CA system is that any CA - even the most incompetent - can sign certificates for any domain. If trust was moved to DNS, there would only be a single organisation that could forge certificates for any given domain. Using 7 as a private key? What a joke. The CAs aren't worthy of trust.

We already have to trust the domain name registrars anyway, since CAs query them to figure out if you own a domain before signing a certificate. In total, removing CAs would not only simplify the system. But it would allow scoped signatures. And we'd end up needing to trust far fewer actors to have a secure internet.

Today's incident isn't a domain binding issue; it's a key mishandling issue. Elevating the role of TLD operators here just increases the number of organizations we have to trust to handle keys properly; worse, as we agree, those new keyholders can't have their authority revoked.

In the main, attacks on the DV process aren't protocol attacks; they're simple ATO attacks on registrars. The DV part of the WebPKI is certainly gross and could be improved, but evidence from the last 20 years says pretty clearly that the DV process itself is not the most urgent risk in the system.

My first hope is that we continue to ratchet security requirements for CAs upwards, and in doing so wash more and more incompetent operators out.

I gave openclaw a bitcoin wallet and $100 to spend. I told it the $100 was our marketing budget for the month and it should come up with a marketing strategy and then implement it using the budget.

With in minutes it had spent all the budget buying fake follows on an X account that was similar to mine.

Lessons learnt: Most checkout pages have strong anti bot / fraud protection it struggles to get past. Most checkouts require an account which it struggles to register. It can't budget, if you give it money to spend, it will do as you ask and go to work spending it. It doesn't really know what it needs. It wanted to buy a vps despite already having access to a large dedicated server. It doesn't understand value. It wanted to buy the most expensive package because it offered the most features, it through that means its the best value.

In my case I gave it an email account it could sign up with and then used the bitcoin cli to make the payment.

It had its own wallet so it couldn't spend more than what was in it. I didn't want to limit it to for example $10 a day because I wanted it to be able to buy in bulk. Most advert space will be like $70 for a week not $10 a day. So I thought a daily limit would not work unless I put a large budget behind it.

It misses the entire point of money tbh. It just doesn't understand it.

Creating accounts and fraud protection are the biggest issues tbh. We need an alternative to captcha. Something that protects registration and checkout pages from abuse but can still be solved by agents. If you solve that issue the rest is already solved, just give it a credit card or crypto account. Most corporate cc providers allow you to put limits and alerts on the cards.

In a few years that will be the norm but for now I think agent marketplaces are the best solution. Instead of trying to work around bot protection on ebay just make an agent friendly ebay. That's what I am building.

For RDAP to work (for instance) you only need to bootstrap with secure connectivity to the registrars. Current DV challenges have a much harder problem: they have to work with every zone on the Internet. There's no real reason to accept that constraint!

When we think about "sound engineering" this is the level we need to start at, not "what features could we bolt on to core Internet infrastructure to define the problem away".

The people most avidly pushing DNSSEC for this problem aren't stupid. They're just smuggling in an additional premise: that the WebPKI itself is bad, and should be replaced with a DNS PKI. Seen through that lens, secure proof of domain ownership would be deeply problematic, as it would leave the DNS PKI with literally no reason to exist.

comment_text.value:
> Instead of that the ICANN let them go with it based on the flat out lies VeriSign wrote in their request

Unfortunately, I’m not sure if there are actually any lies in their request <https://itp.cdn.icann.org/en/files/consensus-policies/rsep-2...>.

To begin with, the form is really not well-applicable to such requests, but is nonetheless the process that gets used for such things.

Partly because of that, and partly because there are specific meanings of things in the field, there are various things that look like lies, but which aren’t actually. Saying “there will not be any effect on the life cycle of domain names” in §2.1, for example, is technically true: it doesn’t change the life cycle of domain-names-as-a-category, it just deletes a bunch of names (which you could describe as affecting their life cycles!) and removes a category of possible names from registration.

There are also things like §3.6, “Have you communicated with any of the entities whose products or services might be affected by the introduction of your proposed service?” where they just said “no”. (I think most people’s idea that there were lies springs from this section, and misunderstanding that the two sentences of the answer are responding to the two questions; they’re not saying that communicating with people is not applicable.) Irresponsible, and an obvious eyebrow-raiser, but presumably true. My biggest complaint on technicalities would be in §6.2 where they said they consulted with “a select group of registrars comprising a majority of the user base”… whereas I’d consider the registrants to be the user base, and they have said they didn’t consult with them.

§5.1 is perhaps the most ridiculous to me, though, when they say “yeah, our contract says we have to do third-level registrations, we’ll talk about removing that from the contract after discontinuing them”. Probably a part of the procedure, given how they word things, but ludicrous all the same.

They’re also definitely incapable of following instructions. In §5.1 when instructed to write “N/A” they wrote “Not applicable”, and in §7.3 when instructed to write “N/A.” they wrote “None.”

TLDR;

The Danger List

Your robots.txt "Do Not Scrape" signs become legally useless: robots.txt is just a voluntary preference, not a law. While Meta says in PR statements that it will respect robots.txt, it left that promise out of the binding legal contract. By keeping your business account active, you are signing a contract that legally authorizes Meta to ignore your site’s block-lists.

- Meta can create fake accounts to bypass registration walls: The terms explicitly authorize Meta to "create test credentials" to crawl your site. Legal experts warn this gives Meta permission to sign up as a fake user to scrape gated content behind login screens or basic paywalls that anonymous bots usually can't see.

- Your entire domain is fair game, not just links you post: Because the terms cover any domain "associated with your products or services" (or shared by regular users on Meta), Meta isn't just scraping the specific landing pages you run ads for—it has a green light to crawl your entire website from top to bottom.

- AI training is still allowed through a backdoor: Removing the word "train" is a PR smokescreen. The contract still lets Meta scrape your site to "develop, improve, and research... advertising and business products." Because "business products" isn't strictly defined—and Meta builds AI tools for businesses "developing" legally covers training AI models on your proprietary articles, data, and work.

- Third-party companies get the same access: The terms grant these scraping rights to "any entity acting on our behalf," meaning external contractors or third-party scraping vendors hired by Meta also have legal cover to harvest your site.

- It is a non-negotiable hostage situation (Zero Opt-Out): There is no toggle or form to reject this before the October 30 deadline. Your only legal way to decline is to completely delete your commercial presence across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp—forcing you to choose between surrendering your content for free or losing access to your audience.

The Bottom Line: Starting October 30, their updated terms give it sweeping permission to scrape entire websites linked to any Meta Business account (Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp). Despite a last-minute wording tweak after backlash, legal experts warn the rules still let Meta harvest publisher content to build AI tools—with zero option to opt out.

1. What Exact Things Can Meta Do?

If you have a Meta Business account, you authorize Meta (and its third-party partners) to:

a) Deploy automated bots: Use web scrapers, crawlers, spiders, and user agents on your site. b) Bypass basic walls: Create "test credentials" to access, index, cache, analyze, and collect your content. c) Monitor continuously: Periodically pull updates from your domains, web pages, and URLs.

2. What is the Extent of the Scraping? - What gets scraped: Any domain, webpage, URL, or content "associated with" your business or shared by users on Meta platforms. Legal experts note this is broad enough to let Meta scrape entire websites, not just specific landing pages. - - Who it affects: Virtually every news organization and business that uses a Meta account to manage Facebook Pages, Instagram profiles, Threads, or WhatsApp channels.

How it expanded:

  - Previously: Meta could only scrape your site if you specifically used its generative AI ad features, and only to "optimize your ads."
 
  - Now: It applies to all business accounts by default, and scraped data can be used for all "advertising and business products" (plus platform security/integrity).
3. Why Legal Experts Say Meta's "Fix" Changes Nothing After initial outrage, Meta revised the text on Friday to remove the word "train" and claimed it still respects robots.txt (the code websites use to block scrapers). Legal experts aren't buying it for three reasons:

- "Develop" still means "Train": Meta replaced "train" with permission to "develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products." Attorneys point out that "business products" isn't strictly defined, and "developing" AI business tools naturally includes training AI models on your data.

- The robots.txt loophole: While a Meta spokesperson publicly promised to respect robots.txt flags, Meta refused to put that promise into the actual legal terms. Because robots.txt is voluntary, signing a contract that explicitly authorizes scraping legally overrides your robots.txt preferences.

- Take it or leave it: There is no opt-out. To avoid giving Meta permission to scrape their websites, businesses and news outlets would have to abandon Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp entirely before October 30.

If you have a Meta Business account, you authorize Meta (and its third-party partners) to:

a) Deploy automated bots: Use web scrapers, crawlers, spiders, and user agents on your site. b) Bypass basic walls: Create "test credentials" to access, index, cache, analyze, and collect your content. c) Monitor continuously: Periodically pull updates from your domains, web pages, and URLs.

2. What is the Extent of the Scraping? - What gets scraped: Any domain, webpage, URL, or content "associated with" your business or shared by users on Meta platforms. Legal experts note this is broad enough to let Meta scrape entire websites, not just specific landing pages. - - Who it affects: Virtually every news organization and business that uses a Meta account to manage Facebook Pages, Instagram profiles, Threads, or WhatsApp channels.

How it expanded:

  - Previously: Meta could only scrape your site if you specifically used its generative AI ad features, and only to "optimize your ads."
 
  - Now: It applies to all business accounts by default, and scraped data can be used for all "advertising and business products" (plus platform security/integrity).
3. Why Legal Experts Say Meta's "Fix" Changes Nothing After initial outrage, Meta revised the text on Friday to remove the word "train" and claimed it still respects robots.txt (the code websites use to block scrapers). Legal experts aren't buying it for three reasons:

- "Develop" still means "Train": Meta replaced "train" with permission to "develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products." Attorneys point out that "business products" isn't strictly defined, and "developing" AI business tools naturally includes training AI models on your data.

- The robots.txt loophole: While a Meta spokesperson publicly promised to respect robots.txt flags, Meta refused to put that promise into the actual legal terms. Because robots.txt is voluntary, signing a contract that explicitly authorizes scraping legally overrides your robots.txt preferences.

- Take it or leave it: There is no opt-out. To avoid giving Meta permission to scrape their websites, businesses and news outlets would have to abandon Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp entirely before October 30.

That iSeeCars study is shaky. The death counts come from federal data, but miles driven are their own private estimates, so nobody can check the math.

The more rigorous data is the IIHS driver death rates, which use real registration data and adjust for driver age and gender (iihs.org/topics/driver-death-rates). It shows the RWD Model 3 is about half its class average (15 vs 29 deaths per million vehicle-years) and the Model S is about average. The AWD Model 3 is above average (39 vs 29), which points more to how fast cars get driven than to the car itself. IIHS hasn’t published a Model Y rate yet.

So Teslas aren’t the deadliest brand. The faster versions show more risk, which is the same pattern IIHS sees with muscle cars.

First off, that's like asking your building inspectors "what can I do without a permit". Governments are dearth to "help out" like that. Even if you know a guy, the boundaries typically aren't binding until a survey has been done the state or municipality has a approved it and it's been registered with whoever handles land stuff in your jurisdiction.

Second, most states that regulate wetlands beyond the federal minimum adopt some sort of absurd expansive standard far above what the feds want. It's complex and varies by state. Sometimes there's a square footage minimum, sometimes there isn't. There's also "gotchas" where manmade areas can become wetlands if they are let to be that way too long, so like farmer Johnson can absolutely get screwed by his grandfather's bright idea to make all the drainage converge in one spot 40yr ago. Sometimes there are exemptions, sometimes not. There's huge variation by state and some states allow local governments to enforce rules above and beyond the state ones.
